CHAPTER 16

 1Ch 16:1-6 . David's Festival Sacrifice and Liberality to the People.

 2. he blessed the people in the name of the Lord-- The king commended their zeal, supplicated the divine blessing upon them, and ordered the remains of the thank offerings which had been profusely sacrificed during the procession, to be distributed in certain proportions to every individual, that the ceremonial might terminate with appropriate festivities ( De 12:7 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3784"/><div sID="gen5425" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3784"/><hi type="bold">4-6. he appointed certain of the Levites to minister before the ark of the Lord--</hi>No sooner was the ark deposited in its tent than the Levites, who were to officiate in the choirs before it, entered upon their duties. A select number of the musicians were chosen for the service from the list (<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19-1Chr.15.21">1Ch 15:19-21</reference>) of those who had taken a prominent part in the recent procession. The same arrangement was to be observed in their duties, now that the ark again was stationary; Asaph, with his associates, composing the first or principal company, played with cymbals; Zechariah and his colleagues, with whom were conjoined Jeiel and Obed-edom, forming the second company, used harps and similar instruments. <div eID="gen5425" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3787"/><div sID="gen5429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3787"/><hi type="bold">7. Then on that day David delivered first this psalm--</hi>Among the other preparations for this solemn inauguration, the royal bard had composed a special hymn for the occasion. Doubtless it had been previously in the hands of Asaph and his assistants, but it was now publicly committed to them as they entered for the first time on the performance of their sacred duties. It occupies the greater part of this chapter (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.8-1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:8-36</reference>), and seems to have been compiled from other psalms of David, previously known to the Israelites, as the whole of it will be found, with very slight variations, in Psa 96:1-13; 105:1-15; 106:47,48. In the form, however, in which it is given by the sacred historian, it seems to have been the first psalm given for use in the tabernacle service. Abounding, as it does, with the liveliest ascriptions of praise to God for the revelation of His glorious character and the display of His marvellous works and containing, as it does, so many pointed allusions to the origin, privileges, and peculiar destiny of the chosen people, it was admirably calculated to animate the devotions and call forth the gratitude of the assembled multitude. <div eID="gen5429" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3788"/><div sID="gen5430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3788"/><hi type="bold">36. all the people said, Amen--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.72.19">Psa 72:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">106:48</reference>). In the former, the author of the doxology utters the "amen" himself, while in the latter the people are exhorted to say "amen." This may arise from the fact that the latter psalm originally concluded with the injunction to say "amen." But in this historical account of the festival, it was necessary to relate that the people obeyed this injunction on the occasion referred to, and therefore the words "let them praise," were altered into "and they praised" [Bertheau]. <div eID="gen5430" type="x-p"/>
